terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Build the ticket program here, run it, and read what it prints.

tasks.title: Print the ticket line
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1` in `src/ticket.cpp`, print the ticket line built from the variables `ticketNumber`, `item` and `customer`. For today's slip it reads:

```
Ticket 2187: carriage clock for Edwina Sallow
```

Check builds and runs your program with other tickets in those variables, and looks for the line each one should give, on a line of its own.
nextSteps: Read the variables at the top of `main`: their names, types and values.
Start a print with `std::cout` and send the first word as text.
Send each variable by its name, with the words between them as text.
Build, run, and compare the line with the task, spaces included.
hints: One `std::cout` can print several pieces, each after its own `<<`.
A variable is sent by its name, without quotes. The words between the variables are text, in double quotes, with their spaces inside the quotes.
The line has the shape `std::cout << "Ticket " << ticketNumber << ": " << ... << "\n";`.

tasks.title: Note where the clock waits
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 2`, make an `int` called `bench` that holds `4`, and a `char` called `shelf` that holds the letter `B`. Then print them from those two variables:

```
Bench 4, shelf B
```

Check reads both variables and their types after your Task 2 lines, looks for the line, and reads your code to see that it prints the variables by their names.
nextSteps: Write the type, the name, `=`, the value and a semicolon for `bench`.
Do the same for `shelf`. One character has its own kind of quotes.
Print the line, sending `bench` and `shelf` by their names.
Build and run, and read the line.
hints: A variable is made with its type first, then its name, then `=` and its value.
A whole number has no quotes. One character goes in single quotes, and text goes in double quotes.
The two lines have the shapes `int bench = ...;` and `char shelf = '.';`.

tasks.title: Add the key to the quote
tasks.description:
Edwina lost the winding key too. Under `// Task 3`, give `quote` a new value: what it holds now plus `keyPrice`. Do not make a new variable. Then print it:

```
Quote: 82.75
```

Check runs your program with other quotes and key prices, reads `quote` after your Task 3 lines and looks for the line.
nextSteps: Find where `quote` is made, above Task 1. It already exists.
Under Task 3, give it a new value with `=`, using its own name and `keyPrice` on the right.
Build and run: the quote should have gone up by the price of the key.
hints: A variable that already exists is not made again. Putting a type in front of its name makes a second one, and the compiler refuses that.
On the right of `=`, the variable still holds its old value. The new value is stored once the line is done.
The line has the shape `quote = quote + ...;`.

tasks.title: Give daysLeft a value
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 4`, `daysLeft` is made without a value and then printed, so the program prints whatever was left in memory. Give it the value of `promisedDays` on the line that makes it, and keep the line that prints it.

Check reads your code to see that `daysLeft` has its value before it is printed, then runs your program with other promised days and reads `daysLeft` and the line `Ready in ... days`.
nextSteps: Build and run the program a few times and look at the number of days.
Read the warning the compiler gives about the line that prints it.
Give `daysLeft` the value of `promisedDays` where it is made.
Build and run: the warning is gone and the days are the promised ones.
hints: The compiler warns about this line for a reason. Read what it says about `daysLeft`.
A variable made without a value holds whatever was in that memory before. It gets a value with `=` on the line that makes it.
The line has the shape `int daysLeft = ...;`, with the name of the promised days on the right.
